title: The horse the size of the sky
hook: the Brihadaranyaka opens by turning a king's horse sacrifice into the whole universe, so anyone can take part
carry: the whole world is the sacred offering
tomorrow: in the beginning there was nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, after a hundred and one years, Indra learned the self is the one who sees through the eye. That closed the Chandogya.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS AGAIN — THE ONE WHO SEES THROUGH THE EYE.`

segments.voice: A king's horse, turned loose under guard. That's how tradition describes the start of the ashvamedha, the royal horse sacrifice. The horse wandered, the accounts say, for a year, and the lands it crossed were claimed for the king unless someone fought to stop it. Then came the sacrifice itself. And with this horse, a new Upanishad begins: the Brihadaranyaka. Not with the ritual's rules, though, or its costs. With a vision.
screen: `THE KING'S HORSE, FREE FOR A YEAR.` → `WHEREVER IT WALKS, THE KING CLAIMS.` → `NOT RULES. A VISION.`

segments.voice: Its first words, in Sanskrit, are usha va ashvasya medhyasya shirah. The dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse. Then it keeps going, part by part. The sun is its eye. The wind, its breath. The universal fire, its open mouth. The year is its body. The sky is its back, the air between earth and sky its belly. The stars are its bones, the clouds its flesh, the rivers its entrails, the plants and trees its hair. When it yawns, that's lightning. When it shakes itself, thunder. When it makes water, rain. And its neighing is speech. Read slowly, it's a portrait of the whole world in the shape of one animal. Here's the big turn in Hinduism this passage shows. The Upanishads don't throw out the old fire rituals. They carry them inside: the sacrifice becomes something you see and understand. Teachers call this kind of meditation upasana, and many read this opening as one: you don't need a king's horse, because the whole world is already the offering. Dawn breaks across its head every morning. Its breath is the wind on your face. That's part of why a Hindu can stand at sunrise, no priest, no fire, and still be at worship. Brihadaranyaka means the great forest teaching. It belongs to the White Yajur Veda. In the coming weeks it brings us to Yajnavalkya, and to the philosopher Gargi. But it starts here: at sunrise, with a horse the size of the sky.
screen: `USHA VA ASHVASYA MEDHYASYA SHIRAH.` · `SUN ITS EYE, WIND ITS BREATH.` · `THE RITUAL, CARRIED INSIDE.` · `THE GREAT FOREST TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD IS THE OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Picture the sky at dawn, the first light along the horizon: the horse's head. Feel the air on your skin as its breath, and let the clouds, the rivers you know and the trees outside take their places as its flesh, its entrails, its hair. If you pray, many Hindus greet the rising sun with a bow or a little water poured toward it; you can bow inwardly now. If you don't, simply breathe, and let the whole world feel like one sacred body, with you somewhere inside it.
Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice. The Brihadaranyaka opens by seeing the sacrificial horse as the universe: the dawn its head, the sun its eye, the wind its breath.
Your line: the whole world is the sacred offering. Tomorrow, a stranger first sentence: in the beginning, nothing. See you then.

howItsDone: The ashvamedha is rarely if ever performed today, but the Brihadaranyaka is studied in Vedic schools of the White Yajur Veda and by Vedanta students, and its opening is often read as a meditation on the world as one sacred body.

notes: Opens the Brihadaranyaka (part open). Sanskrit of 1.1.1 in simplified transliteration (uṣā vā aśvasya medhyasya śiraḥ); confirm.

Correspondences paraphrased from 1.1.1: dawn head, sun eye, wind breath, Vaishvanara fire open mouth, year body (atman), sky back, atmosphere belly, stars bones, clouds flesh, rivers veins, plants and trees hair, yawn lightning, shaking thunder, urinating rain, neighing speech. Confirm each; some translators vary.
Ashvamedha description (horse roams a year, guarded; land claimed) is the standard account; confirm.

'Taught in the forest, tradition says' for aranyaka: softened; confirm. Gargi and Yajnavalkya are previewed as later in the Brihadaranyaka (books 2–4); confirm they fall within the outline's 28 sessions.
